questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit apply Fifth Circuit law for JMOL review but its own law for claim construction?
questions.question_body: In this opinion, the court says it reviews the denial of JMOL under the law of the regional circuit (Fifth Circuit), but then says it reviews claim construction de novo and any underlying factual findings for clear error. I understand the Federal Circuit has nationwide jurisdiction over patent appeals, but I'm confused about how it decides which body of procedural law to apply. Why is JMOL review governed by regional circuit law while claim construction follows Federal Circuit precedent? Is there a principled basis for this split, or is it just historical accident?

questions.title: When is expert testimony so self-contradictory that it cannot support a jury verdict?
questions.question_body: The court reverses the JMOL denial on the '134 patent because Dr. Wells' testimony was "confusing and unclear" and he gave contradictory testimony about whether the "interference generating signals" mapped to the modeled PIM path or to x1 and x2. The court cites Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope Corp. for the proposition that self-contradictory expert testimony cannot support a jury verdict. But I thought credibility determinations and weighing conflicting testimony were jury functions. At what point does contradictory expert testimony cross the line from a credibility issue for the jury to insufficient evidence as a matter of law? Is there a specific test, or is it just case-by-case judgment?

questions.title: How does the "clear and unambiguous disavowal" standard apply when a patentee narrows claim language during prosecution?
questions.question_body: On the '775 patent, the appellants argued Finesse surrendered claim scope over two-signal products when it amended the claims from "two or three signals" to "three signals" during prosecution to overcome the Filipovic reference. The court disagreed, saying the amendment doesn't rise to the level of "clear and unambiguous" disavowal under Continental Circuits v. Intel. But I'm confused about the boundary here. The patentee changed "two or three" to "three"—that seems like a deliberate narrowing. What distinguishes a routine claim amendment from a "clear and unambiguous" disavowal? Does the standard require the patentee to explicitly disavow scope, or can disavowal be inferred from the amendment itself combined with the prosecution context?

questions.title: What does it mean for signals to be "separately identifiable" but not "unique" in patent claim construction?
questions.question_body: The district court construed "three signals S1, S2 and S3" in the '775 patent to be "separately identifiable" but not "unique." The Federal Circuit seemed to accept this construction. I'm struggling with what this actually means in practice. If S1, S2, and S3 can be the same signal (not unique), in what sense are they "separately identifiable"? Can you give an example of signals that are separately identifiable but not unique? Is this saying you can use two distinct signals and a copy of one of them, as the district court found? What is the practical significance of this distinction for infringement analysis?

questions.title: Why was the argument that S1, S2, and S3 must be "unique" signals found waived, and what is the Rule 50(a) waiver requirement?
questions.question_body: The district court rejected AT&T's argument that "S1, S2 and S3" must be unique signals as "waived" because they failed to raise it at the Rule 50(a) stage. I'm confused about the procedural mechanics here. What is the Rule 50(a) stage, and what exactly must a party do to preserve an issue for JMOL? Is there a difference between what must be argued in a Rule 50(a) motion before the case goes to the jury versus a Rule 50(b) motion after the verdict? If you don't raise an argument in 50(a), are you completely barred from raising it in 50(b) and on appeal, or are there exceptions?

questions.title: Why is the damages award vacated rather than just remanded for recalculation when infringement is reversed?
questions.question_body: At the end of the opinion, the court says it vacates the damages award because it reversed the denial of JMOL of noninfringement for all asserted claims. I understand that if there's no infringement, there should be no damages, but I'm confused about the procedural mechanics. Why vacate rather than reverse? What's the difference between vacating a damages award and reversing it? And does this mean the entire damages issue is moot, or could there be some scenario where damages survive even partially if some claims or theories of infringement had been upheld?

questions.title: How does the substantial evidence standard interact with an expert's failure to map accused product features to specific claim limitations?
questions.question_body: On the '775 patent, Dr. Wells identified three distinct multiplications in the Nokia document but never testified how those three map onto the seven claimed multiplications. Finesse tried to provide this mapping for the first time on appeal. The court held no reasonable jury could find infringement. I'm trying to understand the evidentiary standard here. If the expert testified the accused product infringes, isn't it the jury's role to decide whether that testimony is credible? When does an expert's failure to provide a specific element-by-element mapping become insufficient as a matter of law versus just a weak case for the jury to weigh? What if the jury could have inferred the mapping itself?
